claim: Homeostatic systems that rely on genetic regulatory networks are intrinsically limited by the transcriptional response time.
source: Homeostatic systems that rely on genetic regulatory networks are intrinsically limited by the transcriptional response time, which may restrict a cell's ability to adapt to unanticipated environmental challenges.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general principle about homeostatic systems.

claim: Exposure to mild stress increases cellular resistance to subsequent threats.
source: To bypass this limitation, cells have evolved mechanisms whereby exposure to mild stress increases their resistance to subsequent threats.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established phenomenon.

claim: Acquisition of tolerance is a systems-level property resulting from nonlinearity of H2O2 scavenging by peroxiredoxins.
source: We demonstrate that acquisition of tolerance is a systems-level property resulting from nonlinearity of H2O2 scavenging by peroxiredoxins
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data and modeling throughout the manuscript.

claim: The nonlinear regulatory scheme induces a hormetic effect of extracellular H2O2 stress on replicative longevity.
source: our study reveals that this regulatory scheme induces a striking hormetic effect of extracellular H2O2 stress on replicative longevity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by replicative lifespan experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Bacterial chemotaxis is a perfectly adapting system based on integral feedback.
source: Several seminal studies have pointed to the existence of 'perfectly adapting' systems in which exact restoration of the pre-existing state is observed, including bacterial chemotaxis (Barkai and Leibler, 1997; Berg and Tedesco, 1975), calcium signaling (El-Samad et al., 2002), and yeast hyperosmolarity response (Muzzey et al., 2009), all of which are based on a regulatory scheme referred to as 'integral feedback' (Yi et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Calcium signaling is a perfectly adapting system based on integral feedback.
source: Several seminal studies have pointed to the existence of 'perfectly adapting' systems in which exact restoration of the pre-existing state is observed, including bacterial chemotaxis (Barkai and Leibler, 1997; Berg and Tedesco, 1975), calcium signaling (El-Samad et al., 2002), and yeast hyperosmolarity response (Muzzey et al., 2009), all of which are based on a regulatory scheme referred to as 'integral feedback' (Yi et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Yeast hyperosmolarity response is a perfectly adapting system based on integral feedback.
source: Several seminal studies have pointed to the existence of 'perfectly adapting' systems in which exact restoration of the pre-existing state is observed, including bacterial chemotaxis (Barkai and Leibler, 1997; Berg and Tedesco, 1975), calcium signaling (El-Samad et al., 2002), and yeast hyperosmolarity response (Muzzey et al., 2009), all of which are based on a regulatory scheme referred to as 'integral feedback' (Yi et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Most stress regulatory pathways feature transcriptional responses which are intrinsically slower processes than other biochemical effects of stress exposure.
source: indeed, most stress regulatory pathways feature transcriptional responses, which are intrinsically slower processes than the other biochemical effects of stress exposure (Muzzey and van Oudenaarden, 2009; Young et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A transient peak in internal stress level may occur in response to stepwise exposure to an external stressor due to limiting response time.
source: Because of this limiting response time, it is expected that a transient peak in the internal stress level (output peak of magnitude Omax, Figure 1A) may occur in response to stepwise exposure to an external stressor (input, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the properties of homeostatic systems, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The rate at which stress is applied should directly control the maximum internal stress level and determine cellular stress resistance.
source: In this case, interestingly, the rate at which stress is applied (while keeping constant the overall magnitude of stress) should directly control Omax and hence determine cellular stress resistance (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The hypothesis that adaptation range depends on the kinetics of the input stress pattern has neither been formally addressed theoretically nor tested experimentally.
source: Remarkably, this hypothesis has neither been formally addressed theoretically nor been tested experimentally.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature.

claim: Acquired stress resistance has been observed in a broad spectrum of species from unicellular organisms to mammals in response to diverse environmental challenges.
source: This effect has been observed in a broad spectrum of species, from unicellular organisms to mammals, in response to diverse environmental challenges (Davies et al., 1995; Hecker et al., 2007; Kandror et al., 2004; Kensler et al., 2007; Lewis et al., 1995; Lindquist, 1986; Lou and Yousef, 1997; Lu et al., 1993; Scholz et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Stress resistance is an anticipation strategy to overcome potentially harmful environmental conditions in the future.
source: and is considered to be an anticipation strategy to overcome potentially harmful environmental conditions in the future (Mitchell et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Cells rapidly degrade H2O2 in the medium during standard adaptation assays.
source: Adaptation to H2O2 is usually measured by quantifying the fraction of surviving cells after the addition of a bolus of H2O2 to cells in culture. Under these conditions, cells rapidly degrade the H2O2 in the medium and, therefore, adaptation is partly due to the removal of the stressor.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of standard assays.

claim: A custom microfluidic device was developed to monitor divisions of individual cells while controlling external H2O2 concentrations by continuous replenishment.
source: To circumvent this problem and to allow precise control of the stressor level, we developed custom microfluidic device to monitor the divisions of individual cells in trapping cavities while controlling external H2O2 concentrations by continuous replenishment of H2O2-containing medium (Figure 1B and C and Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a methodological development described in the text and shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Diffusion in the trapping cavities was not impaired by the presence of a large cell cluster.
source: Using a fluorescent dye, we checked that diffusion in the trapping cavities was not impaired by the presence of a large cell cluster in the cavity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Cell growth was not affected by increasing cell confinement during a typical experiment up to 1000 min.
source: and we also verified that cell growth was not affected despite the increasing cell confinement during a typical experiment (up to 1000 min, see Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Yap1 is a transcription factor that shuttles between the cytoplasm and nucleus in the absence of H2O2.
source: Yap1 is a transcription factor that, in the absence of H2O2, shuttles between the cytoplasm and nucleus.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Yap1 function.

claim: Upon exposure to H2O2, Yap1 is oxidized and nuclear export is prevented.
source: Upon exposure to H2O2, Yap1 is oxidized and nuclear export is prevented (Azevedo et al., 2003; Kuge et al., 1997; Lee et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Nuclear accumulation of Yap1 is a sensitive reporter of internal H2O2 levels.
source: Hence, nuclear accumulation of Yap1 is a sensitive reporter of internal H2O2 levels (Toledano et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Yap1 activates the expression of genes involved in redox homeostasis and H2O2 scavenging.
source: In the nucleus, Yap1 activates the expression of genes involved in redox homeostasis and H2O2 scavenging (Gasch et al., 2000; Godon et al., 1998; Lee et al., 1999), leading to a negative feedback regulatory loop (Toledano et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cells experienced a transient stress level-dependent reduction in growth rate followed by complete recovery after switching to H2O2-containing medium.
source: Following the switch to medium containing 0–0.4 mM H2O2 (at t = 300 min; Figure 1D and Video 1), the cells experienced a transient stress level-dependent reduction in growth rate (see Materials and methods for the principle of the measurement) followed by a complete recovery, revealing intrinsic cellular adaptation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The switch to H2O2 induced an abrupt burst in Yap1-GFP nuclear localization which saturated above 0.2 mM H2O2.
source: In parallel, the switch to H2O2 induced an abrupt burst in Yap1-GFP nuclear localization, which saturated above 0.2 mM H2O2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The nuclear relocation time of Yap1 is around 120 seconds.
source: Similar experiments performed with higher temporal resolution (30 s interval) revealed that the nuclear relocation time is around 120 s (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The activation of Yap1 is set by the diffusion of the stressor across the cell membrane rather than by limited diffusion in the device.
source: However, this stands significantly higher than the timescale of stressor diffusion across cavity (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B), therefore revealing that the activation of Yap1 is set by the diffusion of the stressor across the cell membrane rather than by limited diffusion in the device.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing timescales from experimental data.

claim: The burst of nuclear Yap1-GFP relocation was followed by partial recovery to a steady-state level that was H2O2 concentration-dependent.
source: The burst of nuclear Yap1-GFP relocation was followed by partial recovery to a steady-state level that was also H2O2 concentration-dependent (Figure 1D–F and Video 2)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: Yap1 activity is still required in the adapted state following growth recovery.
source: suggesting that Yap1 activity is still required in the adapted state (i.e. following growth recovery).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Yap1 remains partially nuclear at steady state.

claim: Deletion of Yap1 strongly decreased the cells' capacity to adapt.
source: Consistent with this, deletion of Yap1 strongly decreased the cells' capacity to adapt, in agreement with previous findings (Inoue et al., 1999) (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E, and by citation to previous work.

claim: Yap1 signaling is more sensitive to H2O2 than is the overall cellular physiology.
source: Last, the fact that a 0.1 mM H2O2 stress induces a partial nuclear relocation of Yap1-GFP but has no effect on growth rate indicates that Yap1 signaling is more sensitive to H2O2 than is the overall cellular physiology (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Cells adapted to 0.3 mM H2O2 with complete mean growth rate recovery.
source: Interestingly, while the cells adapted to 0.3 mM H2O2 (complete mean growth rate recovery), exposure to 0.6 mM H2O2 induced full growth arrest (Figure 1E and Video 3)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Exposure to 0.6 mM H2O2 induced full growth arrest.
source: Interestingly, while the cells adapted to 0.3 mM H2O2 (complete mean growth rate recovery), exposure to 0.6 mM H2O2 induced full growth arrest (Figure 1E and Video 3)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Cell fate is controlled by a sharp threshold in external H2O2 level.
source: revealing that cell fate is controlled by a sharp threshold in external H2O2 level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of a sharp transition between adaptation and arrest.

claim: At 0.5 mM H2O2, 22% of cells recovered normal growth and division rate (adapted phenotype).
source: 22% of cells present at the time of H2O2 addition recovered a normal growth and division rate at t > 600 min (referred to as the 'adapted' phenotype in the following)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: At 0.5 mM H2O2, 36% of cells experienced prolonged cell cycle arrest phenotype.
source: 36% experienced a prolonged slow-down of cell cycle progression characterized by an extended budded period, but continued to increase in size over time ('prolonged cell cycle arrest' phenotype)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: At 0.5 mM H2O2, 42% of cells stopped growing and failed to divide (permanent growth arrest phenotype).
source: and 42% stopped growing and failed to divide ('permanent growth arrest' phenotype) (Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: The cell cycle arrest phenotype emerged at lower concentrations of H2O2 (~0.2 mM) than the growth arrest phenotype (~0.5 mM).
source: Interestingly, performing the same analysis of phenotypic distribution at various H2O2 levels revealed that the cell cycle arrest phenotype emerged at lower concentrations of H2O2 than the growth arrest phenotype (typically ~0.2 and 0.5 mM H2O2, respectively; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Exposure to 0.4 mM H2O2 substantially increased cytoplasmic Rnr3-GFP levels in cells displaying the prolonged cell cycle arrest phenotype but not in adapted cells.
source: Exposure to 0.4 mM H2O2 substantially increased cytoplasmic Rnr3-GFP levels in cells displaying the prolonged cell cycle arrest phenotype, but not in adapted cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The vast majority of cell-cycle-arrested cells displayed bright foci of Ddc2-GFP fluorescence, unlike adapted cells.
source: Similarly, the vast majority of cell-cycle-arrested cells displayed bright foci of Ddc2-GFP fluorescence, unlike adapted cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: H2O2-induced DNA damage and subsequent DDR checkpoint activation were responsible for prolonged cell cycle arrest.
source: These experiments indicated that H2O2-induced DNA damage and subsequent DDR checkpoint activation were responsible for prolonged cell cycle arrest.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of Rnr3 and Ddc2 markers in cell-cycle-arrested cells.

claim: All cells exposed to 0.6 mM H2O2 eventually became fluorescent with propidium iodide, demonstrating that this stress exposure ultimately induces cell lysis.
source: To test this hypothesis, first, we used a vital stain (propidium iodide, PI) to monitor the onset of death in cells abruptly exposed to 0.6 mM H2O2 (see Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B and Video 5). We found that all cells (N = 123) eventually became fluorescent, therefore demonstrating that a stress exposure to this H2O2 concentration ultimately induces cell lysis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Removal of 0.6 mM H2O2 stress led to recovery of mean cellular growth rate and reactivation of the Yap1 regulon if the duration of exposure was less than 4 hours.
source: However, removal of the stress by switching back to H2O2-free medium at various times after H2O2 addition led to recovery of the mean cellular growth rate and induced reactivation of the Yap1 regulon if the duration of exposure was less than 4 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: A few hours of exposure at 0.6 mM H2O2 were necessary to induce an irreversible growth arrest phenotype that ultimately leads to cell death.
source: This indicated that a few hours of exposure at 0.6 mM H2O2 were necessary to induce an irreversible growth arrest phenotype that ultimately lead to cell death.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reversibility experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The subpopulation of permanently arrested cells at 0.4 mM or 0.6 mM H2O2 showed very low TRX2-GFP levels.
source: For this, we compared the expression of the TRX2-GFP fusion protein following either a 0.4 mM or a 0.6 mM H2O2 step. In both cases, we observed that the subpopulation of permanently arrested cells showed very low TRX2-GFP levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-C.

claim: Permanently arrested cells displayed bright and large vacuole phenotype in both 0.4 mM and 0.6 mM H2O2 conditions.
source: In addition, we found that, unlike adapted and cell cycle arrested cells, cells with a permanent growth arrest displayed the same bright and large vacuole phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C) in both conditions (0.4 mM and 0.6 mM H2O2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-C.

claim: The permanent growth arrest phenotype reflects the inability of the cells to defend against the stressor.
source: Therefore, these results indicate that the permanent growth arrest phenotype observed in step experiments (lethal or sublethal) reflects the inability of the cells to defend against the stressor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of low TRX2-GFP levels and vacuole phenotype in permanently arrested cells.

claim: A linear version of the mathematical model successfully recapitulated the limited accuracy of the homeostatic system.
source: For the sake of simplicity, we first developed a linear version of this model (f(H)=1 and g(H) = H; Figure 3A) that could successfully recapitulate the limited accuracy of the homeostatic system; the internal H2O2 level at steady-state Heq increases with the magnitude of H2O2 steps, unlike a system based on an 'integral' feedback regulatory scheme (Figures 1E, F and 3B, and Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 3B and comparison with experimental data in Figure 1E-F.

claim: The limited accuracy of the homeostatic system is a direct consequence of the assumption that antioxidants must be diluted in growing cells.
source: This property is a direct consequence of the assumption that antioxidants are not infinitely stable but must be diluted in growing cells (μ'≠0, see Materials and methods and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is an inference based on mathematical modeling shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The growth rate does not affect the kinetics of the internal H2O2 burst during the transient response to H2O2 steps.
source: However, the growth rate does not affect the kinetics of the internal H2O2 burst during the transient response to H2O2 steps (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The linear model predicted that slower stress ramps may allow cells to adapt to much higher stress levels than steep ramps.
source: Importantly, the linear model also predicted that, whereas steep ramps would quickly lead to growth arrest (since, eventually Hmax > Htox; green line on Figure 3C and inset), as observed experimentally beyond 0.6 mM, slower stress ramps may allow the cells to adapt to much higher stress levels (keeping Hmax < Htox; blue lines on Figure 3C and inset).
evidence: This is a prediction from the mathematical model shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No decline in growth rate was observed up to >4 mM H2O2 when the ramp slope was ≤4.4 μM/min.
source: Under these conditions, we observed no decline in growth rate up to >4 mM H2O2 when the slope δ was ≤4.4 μM/min (Figure 3D and E)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: The growth rate decreased progressively at ramp slopes ≥8.8 μM/min.
source: whereas the growth rate decreased progressively at δ ≥8.8 μM/min (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Nuclear localization of Yap1 was lower during ramping than during step experiments.
source: In agreement with this, nuclear localization of Yap1 was lower during ramping (Figure 3E) than during the step experiments (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 1E.

claim: The onset of growth decline occurred at a H2O2 concentration of 7.2 mM during a slow ramp (δ = 2.2 μM/min) for >5000 min.
source: To estimate this threshold experimentally, we monitored the growth rate of cells upon exposure to a slow H2O2 ramp (δ = 2.2 μM/min) for >5000 min and found that the onset of growth decline occurred at a H2O2 concentration of 7.2 mM (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F.

claim: There is a >10-fold increase in the H2O2 adaptation limit when using slow versus fast stress ramping.
source: Overall, this analysis identified a > 10-fold increase in the H2O2 adaptation limit observed when using slow versus fast stress ramping, which could be explained by a linear negative feedback model in which the response time of antioxidant expression plays a critical role.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing adaptation limits from step and ramp experiments.

claim: Pretreating cells with 0.2 mM H2O2 shifted the adaptation threshold to ΔI = 1 mM.
source: To transpose these observations using our methodology, we first verified that pretreating cells with I0 = 0.2 mM H2O2 shifted the adaptation threshold to ΔI = 1 mM (Figure 4A and B), contrasting with the ΔI = 0.6 mM threshold obtained for I0 = 0 mM (as shown in Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The increased resistance to stepwise stress exposure following pretreatment is dependent on the Yap1 regulon.
source: In addition, we found that this effect was clearly dependent on the Yap1 regulon, since yap1Δ mutants did not display acquisition of tolerance (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The linear feedback model predicted that both pretreated and naive cells should experience a similar internal peak stress during a subsequent stress challenge.
source: However, this increased resistance to stepwise stress exposure could not be explained by the linear feedback model, which predicted that both pretreated and naive cells should experience a similar internal peak stress during the subsequent stress challenge (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a prediction from the mathematical model shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The transcription rate of the TRX2 promoter during the challenging step was lower than during the pretreatment.
source: To test this hypothesis, we monitored the rate of TRX2pr-GFP-deg accumulation upon exposure to a range of H2O2 steps and found a lower transcription rate of the TRX2 promoter during the challenging step of magnitude ΔI = 0.6–0.8 mM than during the pretreatment of magnitude I0 = 0.2 mM (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The amplitude of the burst in Yap1 nuclear relocation decreased as a function of the pretreatment level.
source: In line with this, we found that the amplitude of the burst in Yap1 nuclear relocation decreased as a function of the pretreatment level I0 (Figure 4E and F, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E, F, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Pretreated cells perceive a lower internal stress level than naive cells.
source: consistent with the lower transcriptional activation of its effector gene TRX2. This indicated that the pretreated cells perceive a lower internal stress level than do naive cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of lower Yap1 nuclear relocation and TRX2 transcription in pretreated cells.

claim: The nonlinear model was able to quantitatively recapitulate the I0-dependent reduction in peak internal H2O2 during the challenge step.
source: Thus, unlike the linear model, this nonlinear model was able to quantitatively recapitulate the clear I0-dependent reduction in peak internal H2O2 during the challenge step (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and F), the magnitude of which was similar to the experimentally observed Yap1-GFP nuclear relocation (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and F and comparison with experimental data in Figure 4F.

claim: Buffering of slow external fluctuations in H2O2 levels through cellular training is a generic property of homeostatic systems based on negative feedback loops.
source: Finally, computing the phase diagram for the nonlinear model revealed that, whereas buffering of slow external fluctuations in H2O2 levels (i.e. through cellular training) is a generic property of homeostatic systems based on negative feedback loops, the adaptation to fast fluctuations in the external stressor levels following stress preconditioning (i.e. through acquisition of stress tolerance), is a distinct property that requires a specific nonlinear scavenging model (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the phase diagrams for linear and nonlinear models shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Adaptation to fast fluctuations in external stressor levels following stress preconditioning requires a specific nonlinear scavenging model.
source: Finally, computing the phase diagram for the nonlinear model revealed that, whereas buffering of slow external fluctuations in H2O2 levels (i.e. through cellular training) is a generic property of homeostatic systems based on negative feedback loops, the adaptation to fast fluctuations in the external stressor levels following stress preconditioning (i.e. through acquisition of stress tolerance), is a distinct property that requires a specific nonlinear scavenging model (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the phase diagrams for linear and nonlinear models shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Deletion of Yap1 abolished adaptation during stress ramps.
source: Deletion of Yap1 abolished adaptation (Figure 5B) with onset of growth arrest occurring at ~0.1 mM H2O2 (Figure 5C), similar to the threshold observed in step experiments (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The msn2Δmsn4Δ mutant adapted efficiently during stress ramps.
source: The complete absence of 'trainability' of the Yap1 mutant contrasted with the efficient adaptation of the msn2Δmsn4Δ mutant (Figure 5B), which lacks the transcription factors involved in the general stress response.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Mutants lacking erg3 and erg6 adapted perfectly during stress ramps.
source: Similarly, mutants lacking enzymes involved in membrane lipid biosynthesis, erg3Δ and erg6Δ, adapted perfectly (Figure 5B), thus ruling out the possibility that reduced membrane permeability is responsible for adaptation to H2O2 ramps (Branco et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and citation to previous work.

claim: Deletion of Ccp1, Ctt1, or Cta1 did not prevent adaptation during stress ramps.
source: Interestingly, we found that deletion of known H2O2 scavengers, such as the mitochondrial cytochrome c peroxidase Ccp1 or the cytosolic and peroxisomal catalases Ctt1 and Cta1, did not contribute to adaptation (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Growth recovery was delayed in the ccp1Δ mutant compared with wild-type cells following exposure to 0.4 mM H2O2.
source: Indeed, growth recovery was delayed in the ccp1Δ mutant (but not the ctt1Δcta1Δ mutant) compared with wild-type cells following exposure to a single dose of 0.4 mM H2O2 (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Some H2O2 scavengers may actively contribute to the transient stress response even if they are not implicated in overall H2O2 homeostasis.
source: This finding indicates that some H2O2 scavengers may actively contribute to the transient stress response even if they are not implicated in overall H2O2 homeostasis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ccp1Δ shows delayed recovery in step experiments but adapts normally in ramp experiments.

claim: Simultaneously deleting the three peroxiredoxin genes TSA1, TSA2, and AHP1 abolished cell growth during exposure to H2O2 as ramps or steps.
source: In contrast, simultaneously deleting the three peroxiredoxin genes TSA1, TSA2, and AHP1, which encode the two yeast 2-Cys Prxs and the atypical Prx Ahp1 (tsa1Δtsa2Δahp1Δ), abolished cell growth whether the cells were exposed to H2O2 as ramps or as steps (Figure 5D and E, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: The extent of adaptation was proportional to the number of cytosolic Prxs present.
source: Additionally, the extent of adaptation was proportional to the number of cytosolic Prxs present (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Constitutive expression of Tsa1 under the ACT1 promoter in a tsa1Δ tsa2Δ background did not complement Tsa1 function.
source: Constitutive expression of Tsa1 under the ACT1 promoter (albeit less effective than the endogenous promoter, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B) in a tsa1Δ tsa2Δ background did not complement Tsa1 function, indicating the importance of the H2O2-dependent transcriptional induction of the corresponding effector genes (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Peroxiredoxins are the essential antioxidants ensuring H2O2 homeostasis.
source: Altogether, these observations demonstrate that Prxs are the essential antioxidants ensuring H2O2 homeostasis (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Adaptation was severely compromised in the trx1Δtrx2Δ strain.
source: To determine which of the two Tsa1 functions is involved in adaptation to stress ramps, we first tested a mutant lacking the two cytosolic Trxs (trx1Δtrx2Δ) that assist Prxs in H2O2 scavenging, but not in protein quality control (PQC). We observed that adaptation was severely compromised in this strain (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The tsa1C171Stsa2Δ strain adapted poorly to H2O2.
source: Next, we examined a strain lacking Tsa2 and carrying a TSA1 mutation that impairs the peroxidatic cycle of Prx but not its function in PQC (tsa1C171Stsa2Δ) (Hanzén et al., 2016), and found that this strain also adapted poorly to H2O2 (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H and citation to previous work.

claim: The tsa1ΔYFtsa2Δ strain displayed a wild-type adaptation response.
source: However, a strain lacking Tsa2 and carrying a TSA1 mutation that prevents hyperoxidation and specifically impairs the enzyme's PQC function (tsa1ΔYFtsa2Δ) displayed a wild-type adaptation response (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The Δsrx1 strain displayed wild-type adaptation to H2O2.
source: Lastly, we tested the Δsrx1 strain, in which the defective reduction of hyperoxidized Tsa1 and Tsa2 severely impairs H2O2 scavenging in classical techniques (Biteau et al., 2003) and which Prx-mediated PQC is also defective (Hanzén et al., 2016). Surprisingly, the Δsrx1 strain displayed wild-type adaptation to H2O2 (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H and citations to previous work.

claim: The peroxidatic, not the chaperone, function of 2-Cys Prxs is required for adaptation to stress ramps.
source: Taken together, this genetic analysis indicated that the peroxidatic, not the chaperone, function of 2-Cys Prxs is required for adaptation to stress ramps.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The ramp protocol allows the cell to maintain internal H2O2 at low levels, thereby preventing Tsa1 and Tsa2 hyperoxidation.
source: The dispensability of Srx1 for adaptation suggests that the ramp protocol allows the cell to maintain internal H2O2 at low levels, thereby preventing Tsa1 and Tsa2 hyperoxidation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Δsrx1 adapts normally in ramp experiments.

claim: A sustained increase in cytoplasmic Tsa1-GFP levels was observed upon exposure to a 0.4 mM H2O2 step.
source: Indeed, a sustained increase in cytoplasmic Tsa1-GFP levels was observed upon exposure to a 0.4 mM H2O2 step (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Tsa1-GFP upregulation was accompanied by formation of fluorescent foci.
source: This upregulation was accompanied by formation of fluorescent foci, as noted in previous studies with Tsa1-GFP (Hanzén et al., 2016; Weids and Grant, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous work.

claim: Steady-state Tsa1 levels did not scale linearly with H2O2 concentration, especially at low H2O2 concentrations.
source: However, from the quantitative analysis of the dynamics of Tsa1-GFP protein upregulation (Figure 6B and C) and transcriptional activation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B) upon H2O2 stress, we found that steady-state Tsa1 levels did not scale linearly, especially at low H2O2 concentrations (Figure 6C inset).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B, C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The scaling of Tsa1-GFP expression during a ramp experiment was sublinear.
source: Similarly, the scaling of Tsa1-GFP expression during a ramp experiment (δ = 1.1 μM/min) was sublinear (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The nonlinear model provides a better fit to Tsa1-GFP and Yap1-GFP data than the linear model.
source: These observations were in very good agreement with the nonlinear model, further ruling out the linear model (Figure 6B–D), and the steady-state Yap1-GFP level was also best fit using the nonlinear model (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by comparing model fits to experimental data in Figure 6B-D and Figure 1F.

claim: The H2O2 scavenging capacity of the homeostatic system becomes increasingly more efficient with the accumulation of Prxs as the stress level increases.
source: These results suggest that the H2O2 scavenging capacity of the homeostatic system becomes increasingly more efficient with the accumulation of Prxs as the stress level increases, so that Prxs do not need to be upregulated in proportion to the external H2O2 concentration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nonlinear scaling of Tsa1 expression with H2O2 concentration.

claim: The transcriptional output of cells challenged 400 min after pretreatment was identical to that of cells exposed to H2O2 for the first time.
source: Notably, the transcriptional output of cells challenged 400 min after pretreatment was identical to that of cells exposed to H2O2 for the first time, indicating that the cells had returned to a naïve state by 400 min (Figure 6E upper panel: green vs red lines, and histogram).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: TRX2pr-sfGFP transcription was lower in cells challenged 100 min after pretreatment compared with naive cells.
source: In contrast, TRX2pr-sfGFP transcription was lower in cells challenged 100 min after pretreatment compared with naive cells (Figure 6E, blue vs pink lines, and histogram).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Tsa1-GFP levels were comparable to the basal level after a 400-min recovery period, but not after 100 min.
source: In parallel, we also observed that Tsa1-GFP levels were comparable to the basal level after a 400-min recovery period, but not after 100 min (Figure 6F)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Prx levels are tightly associated with the H2O2 buffering efficiency.
source: suggesting that Prx levels are tightly associated with the H2O2 buffering efficiency.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that stress tolerance is lost as Prx levels decline.

claim: The extension of both chronological and replicative longevity by caloric restriction has been shown to be mediated, at least in part, by activation of H2O2-dependent genes.
source: In support of this, the extension of both chronological and replicative longevity by caloric restriction has been shown to be mediated, at least in part, by activation of H2O2-dependent genes (Mesquita et al., 2010; Molin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Tsa1 plays a role in processing of age-related protein aggregates, and overexpression of Tsa1 alone increases longevity through a mechanism involving the PQC machinery.
source: Furthermore, recent work has shown that Tsa1 plays a role in processing of age-related protein aggregates, and overexpression of Tsa1 alone increases longevity through a mechanism involving the PQC machinery (Hanzén et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Exposure to 10 and 25 μM H2O2 significantly increased RLS up to ~25% compared with unstressed cells.
source: Using this technique, we observed that H2O2 had a biphasic effect on RLS. Exposure to 10 and 25 μM H2O2 significantly increased RLS up to ~25% compared with unstressed cells (median RLS generations of 26, 33, and 32 at 0, 10, and 25 μM H2O2 respectively)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: Concentrations > 50 μM H2O2 decreased RLS.
source: whereas concentrations > 50 μM H2O2 decreased RLS (median RLS of 25 and 20 generations at 50 and 100 μM H2O2, respectively; Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: H2O2 had a hormetic effect on RLS, in which low doses were beneficial and improved RLS, whereas higher doses had deleterious consequences on longevity.
source: This suggested that H2O2 had a hormetic effect, in which low doses of H2O2 were beneficial and improved RLS, whereas higher doses had deleterious consequences on longevity (Ristow and Schmeisser, 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the biphasic effect of H2O2 on RLS shown in Figure 7C and D, and supported by citation to previous work on hormesis.

claim: Deletion of Yap1 or Tsa1 abolished the increase in longevity at low H2O2 doses.
source: We next determined whether this effect was dependent on activation of the H2O2 homeostatic core machinery. Deletion of Yap1 or Tsa1 abolished the increase in longevity at low H2O2 doses (Figure 7E), implicating these proteins in the hormetic effect.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The fraction of cells with foci of Ddc2-GFP and Hsp104-GFP was similar to the unstressed control up to 25 μM H2O2.
source: Indeed, the fraction of cells with foci of Ddc2-GFP (DDR marker) and Hsp104-GFP (protein aggregate marker) was similar to the unstressed control up to 25 μM H2O2 (Figure 7F and G)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F and G.

claim: Tsa1 level experienced a ~25% increase in the range of 0-25 μM H2O2.
source: while Tsa1 level experienced a ~ 25% increase in this range of concentration (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Above 25 μM H2O2, the increase in Tsa1 expression was relatively lower than the increase in damage marker foci.
source: Above 25 μM H2O2, however, the increase in Tsa1 expression was relatively lower than the increase in foci (Figure 7F and G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F and G.

claim: Nonlinear activation of the homeostatic machinery in response to H2O2 leads to a biphasic effect on replicative longevity.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that nonlinear activation of the homeostatic machinery in response to H2O2 leads to a biphasic effect on replicative longevity as recapitulated on Figure 7G.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Many discrepancies in studies of cellular resistance to H2O2 using classical bulk techniques originate from lack of environmental control and population size-dependent consumption of the stressor.
source: Indeed, it is likely that many of the discrepancies observed in studies of cellular resistance to H2O2 using classical bulk techniques originate from both the lack of environmental control and the population size-dependent consumption of the stressor by the cells growing in a test tube or on a plate.
evidence: This is speculation based on the authors' understanding of limitations in previous methodologies.

claim: The final H2O2 concentration and its rate of increase share equal importance in determining cell fate.
source: Our methodology provides a rationalization of H2O2 resistance assays, in which the final H2O2 concentration and its rate of increase share equal importance in determining cell fate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing stress-rate dependence of adaptation.

claim: The use of customized temporal stress patterns is a unique methodology for unraveling the specific functional role of genes involved in H2O2 homeostasis.
source: The use of customized temporal stress patterns appears to be a unique methodology for unraveling the specific functional role of genes involved in H2O2 homeostasis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic analysis results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Prx activity is the major determinant of H2O2 homeostasis and is essential regardless of the temporal stress pattern.
source: These data, therefore, suggest that Prx activity is the major determinant of H2O2 homeostasis and is essential regardless of the temporal stress pattern
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: CCP1 may only contribute to detoxification during the high transient H2O2 peak that accompanies acute stress.
source: whereas CCP1 may only contribute to detoxification during the high transient H2O2 peak that accompanies acute stress.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ccp1Δ shows delayed recovery in step experiments but adapts normally in ramp experiments.

claim: Trainability is an essential functional property intimately linked to the response time of the underlying regulatory mechanism.
source: Beyond the necessary accuracy of a homeostatic control mechanism, our study stresses that 'trainability' is another essential functional property intimately linked to the response time of the underlying regulatory mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and mathematical modeling.

claim: Cells can be acclimated to much higher stress levels (>10 fold) when the rate of increase is low compared with acute exposure.
source: Training has important physiological implications; namely, that cells can be acclimated to much higher stress levels (>10 fold) when the rate of increase is low compared with acute exposure.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: There is an optimal (i.e., fastest) stress pattern for driving a homeostatic system to its maximal stress-buffering capability.
source: In addition, the framework suggests that there is an optimal (i.e., fastest) stress pattern (following the Hmax = Htox contour line on Figure 3C) for driving a homeostatic system to its maximal stress-buffering capability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phase diagram shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The ability to resist progressively increasing environmental insults resembles the concept of mithridatism.
source: Interestingly, the ability to resist progressively increasing environmental insults resembles the concept of mithridatism, which was originally described as a defense strategy against poisoning, but which has lacked overall biological relevance due to the absence of similar mechanistic evidence (Valle et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental findings to a historical concept, supported by citation.

claim: The study identifies a new form of mithridatism at the cellular scale that could be quantitatively explained by a mathematical description of a generic negative feedback-based regulatory network.
source: In the context of H2O2 stress, our study identifies a new form of mithridatism at the cellular scale that could be quantitatively explained by a mathematical description of a generic negative feedback-based regulatory network.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and mathematical modeling.

claim: Training enables increased adaptation to slow stress fluctuations.
source: Unlike training, which enables increased adaptation to slow stress fluctuations, acquired stress resistance elicits improved survival of preconditioned cells to rapid environmental changes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Acquired stress resistance elicits improved survival of preconditioned cells to rapid environmental changes.
source: Unlike training, which enables increased adaptation to slow stress fluctuations, acquired stress resistance elicits improved survival of preconditioned cells to rapid environmental changes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Prxs are very abundant proteins (~1% of the total dry cellular mass in mammals).
source: Even at basal levels, Prxs are very abundant proteins (~1% of the total dry cellular mass in mammals, [Low et al., 2007])
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Prx expression increases up to fivefold upon exposure to H2O2.
source: and our data show that their expression increases up to fivefold upon exposure to H2O2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The cellular concentration of the reduced form of Prxs always surpasses the internal H2O2 concentration.
source: Therefore, it is likely that the cellular concentration of the reduced form of these enzymes always surpasses the internal H2O2 concentration
evidence: This is speculation based on the abundance of Prxs and the nonlinear model assumptions.

claim: The main hypothesis of the nonlinear model is that the H2O2 scavenging rate of Prxs is limited by the internal H2O2 concentration.
source: and, consequently, the main hypothesis of our nonlinear model is that the H2O2 scavenging rate of Prxs is limited by the internal H2O2 concentration.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis underlying the nonlinear model.

claim: Redox homeostasis relies on extremely abundant stoichiometric enzymes rather than on catalases because nonlinearity in the scavenging rate has important physiological consequences, such as stress tolerance.
source: In the meantime, we speculate that the reason redox homeostasis relies on these extremely abundant stoichiometric enzymes rather than on catalases (which catalyze the dismutation of H2O2), as shown here, is that nonlinearity in the scavenging rate has important physiological consequences, such as stress tolerance.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: The phenomenon of acquired stress resistance illustrates the plasticity of the homeostatic machinery.
source: The phenomenon of acquired stress resistance illustrates the plasticity of the homeostatic machinery and shows that cell survival threshold is not static but may be improved by previous environmental conditioning, following the principles of adaptive homeostasis (Davies, 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results, supported by citation.

claim: Prx genes are also regulated by the transcription factors of the general stress response, Msn2/Msn4.
source: Since Prx genes are also regulated by the transcription factors of the general stress response, Msn2/Msn4
evidence: This is established knowledge about Prx gene regulation.

claim: The induction of tolerance to H2O2 by other stressors may be mediated by the same principles as those described in this study.
source: we envision that the induction of tolerance to H2O2 by other stressors may be mediated by the same principles as those described here.
evidence: This is speculation about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: The effect of H2O2 on longevity provides a striking model of lifespan extension induced by environmental perturbation, similar to the effects of caloric restriction.
source: The effect of H2O2 on longevity provides a striking model of lifespan extension induced by environmental perturbation, similar to the effects of caloric restriction.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental findings to caloric restriction effects.

claim: The observation of hormetic effect of H2O2 on replicative aging complements the previously described hormesis-like effect of H2O2 on chronological aging.
source: Interestingly, this observation not only complements the previously described hormesis-like effect of H2O2 on chronological aging (Mesquita et al., 2010)
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings to previous work, supported by citation.

claim: The H2O2 homeostatic machinery plays a central role in the hormetic effect on longevity.
source: but also suggests a simple mechanistic explanation in which the H2O2 homeostatic machinery plays a central role.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Complex functional properties, such as acquired stress tolerance and hormetic lifespan effects, can only be understood by developing specific approaches that bridge the molecular architecture of regulatory pathways to its quantitative dynamical properties.
source: Therefore, our study emphasizes that complex functional properties, such as acquired stress tolerance and hormetic lifespan effects, can only be understood by developing specific approaches that bridge the molecular architecture of regulatory pathways to its quantitative dynamical properties.
evidence: This is a general conclusion based on the overall study.
